explanation:
## One line

```systemverilog
assign y = sel ? b : a;
```

and the only thing to be careful about is which way round it goes. `sel ? b : a` reads "when `sel`, take `b`" — which is what the specification says. `sel ? a : b` is the same shape with the inputs swapped; it gets four of the eight rows right, which is exactly what chance would give you, and is the commonest way to fail this.

## The three ways to write it

All three describe the same circuit. A synthesiser produces identical logic from any of them, and it is worth seeing that, because "which style" is a question people spend a lot of time on and it matters much less than it looks.

```systemverilog
// 1. a continuous assignment
assign y = sel ? b : a;

// 2. a combinational block
always_comb begin
  if (sel) y = b;
  else     y = a;
end

// 3. written out as gates
assign y = (~sel & a) | (sel & b);
```

The third is what the first two become. A multiplexer is an AND for each input, gated by `sel` and its inverse, with the results ORed together — and that is why a multiplexer is the thing FPGA fabric is built out of: a lookup table *is* a multiplexer whose select lines are the inputs.

## What `assign` means, and what it does not

`assign` is **continuous**. It is not a statement that runs once; it is a permanent relationship. From the moment the simulation starts, any change to `a`, `b` or `sel` immediately recomputes `y`. There is no "when" about it.

That is the whole difference between hardware description and programming, and it is worth sitting with for a minute. In a program, `y = f(a, b)` happens at the moment control reaches it and then it is over. In hardware, it describes a piece of wire and logic that exists for as long as the circuit is powered.

## The one that looks right and is not

```systemverilog
always_comb begin
  if (sel) y = b;
end
```

No `else`. When `sel` is 0 nothing assigns `y`, so it keeps whatever it had — which is memory, in a block that was supposed to have none. A synthesiser builds a **latch** for it, and a latch where you meant a wire is a circuit that holds a value nobody asked it to hold and is very hard to time.

The `follows_a` and `no_latch` checks in the grading testbench exist for exactly this: they change an input that should be ignored, and walk the whole table twice, so a design that holds is caught.

## Reading the waveform

Open the **Waveforms** tab after a run. Four traces: `sel`, `a`, `b` and `y`, each a line that is high or low.

Click anywhere on it to put a cursor down; the values at that instant appear underneath. Walk the cursor with the arrow keys and read `y` against `sel`: every 10 ns the inputs step to the next row of the table, and `y` should change in the same instant — not one step later. A `y` that lags by a step is a latch or a register.

Before the first assignment the traces are drawn as a red band. That is `x`, meaning **unknown** — the simulator does not know what value a signal has until something drives it, and it says so rather than guessing zero. Real hardware powers up in some state; `x` is the simulator refusing to pretend it knows which. You will also meet `z`, drawn in amber, which means **nothing is driving this at all** — a floating wire.

## When a check fails

Each check names the row, what was expected and what your design produced, and the simulated time it happened at. Click the failed check and the waveform cursor moves to that instant, so you can look at what the inputs were when it went wrong — which is almost always more useful than the number itself.

Simulation only: passing says nothing about synthesis, timing or a real device.
